An electoral reform bill is ander the consideration of the Italian Chamber of Deputies. It provides that every man who can real and write, and who pays taxes to the amount of 20 lire per annum, shall have a vote. It will raise the electoral body from 000,000, its present number, to over 2,00G,000.

THROOOII the revolution of time we are on the eve of another Chrietmce, the greeted t festival in the Chriatien calendar. Barring a scorn of years, nine- leen oenearies have ridleti putt since a star wen to be obeerved movieg about the firmament and guiding the foutetepe of a party of faithful men to the humble lodging@ of the Redeemer at Bethlehem. ;Ince as in a more remote age the Israelites in their flight from bondage found guides in a cloud by day and a pillar of fire by night. The celebration of the birth of the Saviour of Mankind will to-morrow be celebrated throughout Christendom by religious obserrancea and thanksgiving, and by holiday-making and rejoicing. The eseociations which hang around the tercet carni- val are deep-ceated in the hearts of the people, sod will endure as long as time shell last. No festival is equal to it in the whole range of pastimee and cele- brations, and none ia looked forward to with the earns intentno and kindly interest as the advent of Old Father Christmas, with hie traditional snowy looks and beard of icicles. Parente, animated by the prea- pect of seeing their beloved once muster on the parental hearth, nod strengthen their love and attachment, weloome the time•horioured festival ; echelara in dis- tant schools bceome esgce, am Christmas apprnaehee, to have done for a time with scholastic drudgery, and In melt if by the iron home at break•neek speed to their homee, there lobe greeted with the caresses, and to receive the seusenable gifts, of parents, and to romp and revel with brothem and Meters ; and sons cad daughtara who, is battling with the difSealtiee and responsibilities of life, have, perchance, been 'mat- tered to all quarters of the compass, grow buoyant with the hope of once more aitting by the cosy fire- side at "home," and enjoying there the creature comforts and the company of the old folks at the festive board, around which they were wont to prattle and gambol in their childhood. It ia a season, too, of universal thcekf ulnem, ned ecernisseration —thank. (einem for fortunre favours, and commiceeration for thoee whcea lot is hardship and penury. It in also a time when the heartstrings are slackened, and mite- ; underetandings and aidinceities are buried in the wassail bowl, ced cerolicee proclaim to all people that the coming of the Redeemer was to bring peer, on earth and good will to men, and to perach the never- ' failing dcetrine, "Love thy neighbour at thyself." The joyousness of Christmastide i. of course, to be I meceured in no small degree by the plexitude of or I eepreitsion in the trade and commerce of the country. In that deck heavy cloud, however, a silver lining is Carairlif in view, and a happier and more preaperons ! ; era is dawning. In the cotton manufacturing districts the greater part of the machinery, rearly three fourths of which was at a standetill twelve months age, is in full work and the healthinem of the cotton trade is each as to have iedured the employers to reetore to the employed • part of the amount by which they were ; driven in the worm days of the trade depreesion to ; reduce the wages. Sir—Art was requ;i;il.l.;;;;;Zution paned at &public I meeting to ante. ths honorary searebtry to • bazaar In aid of St. John's Hospital for Dieeases of thy Skin, I may be pardoned for Joking you to accord me space in your columns to appeal to the public for help. Charles Heade, the eminent author, says, with reference to the charity The fatal murvy, the foul leproav, the maddening ccaeina, ere all akin-diseases, and all far more common than supposed, carrying the sufferers to be despised or shunned, whereas in- ternal maladies invite the boon of sympathy. Take the fate of domestic servants SO afflicted. Their employers dis- miss them, however meritorious, and their frieMle than them; mental despair too often follows, and they say with the Patriarch Job, whore bodily affliction, selectell by know- ledge and malignity in person, was a dimase of the akin ; •my misory is greater than I can bear.' Against each a weight of suffering, shame, and sorrow, what is the speeial provision in our enormous city? I am ammainted only with one small hospital—that ought to be a grert one, mid will be in a year, if the public pleases. This is St. John'e Hospital for Diseases of the Skin in Leiceater-square, where the medical officers premribe on an average for nearly four hundred patients every week. It boa already admitted 25.175 new patients. It is open without payment to all creeds and all reeve, the sole eredentials for admission being disease and:poverty. A I,per front India, a Jew from New York,• labourer from New Zealand, marinere from Germmy, • clerk from France, have been mine of it. inmates." The bearoo will take place in June next. In the meantime, St. Julnes Ilospital labours under a heavy load of debt. I beg, therefore, to let me urge your readers to subscribe now to the hamar fund, and their amounts shall be at once handed over to the hospital. A more deserving charit• does not exist. I ehall also be glad to have the namec of lediee who will work for the bazaar. Contributions may be sent lathe chairman of the hospital, the Right Hon, W. N. Masser, M.P., It. Chester-square. div.head: MEETING OF MINERS AT ST. HELENS.
div.p: MEETING OF MINERS AT ST. HELENS.

On Monday evening a meeting of miner. was held on the Fair Ground, St. Helens, to consider the Employer.' Lie- bility Bill and the wages question. Me. John Gross presided, I and in his addrees said they had sent circular. to the routers asking for en advance of 15 per cent on their wage.. They I had euffered the wages to be at almost starvation point, bus the mastere said they would not advance their wages, be- cause trade was not in a condition to warrant it. The masters held • nreetieg in Liverpool, and they were unani• ' mous that wages were lower than they had ever known them to be before, but Mill they could not afford to rain , them and the day after the meeting. the chairman pub- , fished in the newspapers. statement that they had dropped ' the price of coals several times sines 1877, but had not droppel the men'. wages. If that chairman was telling soota ati whet byl been the state of trade far the last ten years ? In 1870, coals were selling at 3S low a rate as they were to-day. In 1872 they advanced, and got to such a price that the public could not afford to buy them, and the manufacturers could not carry on their weds,'. But in 1877 the price began to get to its old level of 1870 the best coals in St. Helens waste that time telling at 6s. Bd. per ton, and the men's ! wages were 241. per week. 't o-den the men's wages were 11Ss. per week, and coals were selling at 7,8 d. atoll at St. Helms and llaydock, and at Prole, at Ss. 24. The wages were therefore twenty percent. lower, end coals twenty per cent. Ligher than M 1817. But they had not dropped the wages as a bade and informed the public what they were doing, but they had Bent their liretnen and undertook,s round, and everything then could possibly take off they had taken off. At Sankey Brook Colliery, last Wednesday, when the toaster went round to measure, what did he do? This was what he did. Yards he had paid Be. tor he would give only 2s. 4d. for ; what he p iid 2s. 8.1. for he gave 2s. ; what he bad paid Is. lon Is. 4u1.; and instead of 11.4 d. he had given Is. Tint aerious alteration hail been dote without entice. At Pilkington's, two men worked in a plac, and made three fair days wage, end when the task master .1111.9 round, lie said at will give you nothing for it." The mas- ters knew very well that their men were not in • position to: resist anything. If they were united like other tradestnt n,. the masters could not take tkl. off here, and h. off there.l But he hopel the next time they senile • notice for an advance they would give the master. to understand that they would starve, they would perish, if they did not get I an advance according to the price of noels in the nrarket It was no use working tall time if they got nothing for it. ' lln the following day there would be • conferenee I of dele,rates front Lancashire, Derbyshire, Stafford. shire, and North and South Wales, and if the people of those places were in the mind to demand an .Ira/we of 15 per cent, no one could prevent them obtainieg it. Thum miners could stop all the machinery in the country, and then the employem would run after them, and offer them money to resume work. He hoped they would henna fort- night's play at the new year. He advised them not to sign , aby document, but when the new year came in they should play • fortnight Just for their own leisure. With no asso- ciation and no funds, the masters thought they could do what they liked with them, and they were doing so; but, if they were united together, the masters would be helpless. Ile then spoke of the Employers' Liability Bill, and mid the mastem were afraid of it. They did not care about minor accidents ; hut if an explosion happened where 100 lives ware lost they wont,' to pay something like £lO,OOO. There- fore they were going about every colliery, among the men, trying to make terms with them, but if they had trounce of. British mettle In their brains they would scorn to put their hands to the terms the masters offered them. The Legislature had given them protection. and they were sdiing it for nothing. The masters told miners they were respon- sible for the limes of their drawers : but • bigger fallacy wet, never uttered. There was nothing of the sort in the Aet, and if it was really lobe • fought battle let them look the worst in the face. If they had to give way and adopt the insurance clauses after the masters had gone alout under- mining uneducated, yet innocent men, and getting Hem to eign they did not know what, the men should appeal to the House of Commons when Perliament opened, and show what ' the masters were doing to defy the law of the land. Th, must get the act so amended that they cOuld sue the mastm; whether they had signet or not ; and at the end of screw years when the Act expirol if it was not satisfactory the men should appeal Inc an amended Act which would give them more than thee had at present. The reason the masterstlid not like Its to was that it rewired them lore' all noxious gsos from min, and the on.y way to do that was to sink another shaft, and that wae what bc, masters were frightened of. The Act mule the masters ' responsible for the lives of the rner, and it would make them more careful whom they employed as managers and order- lookern and so on. He hoped they would stand by the let. and if they must give wry they should show the Home trecretary, the Prime Minister, and Parliament their grie- vance, end how they must starve or sign the masters' document. He asked them to sign nothing till the new year, and it was unanimously carried that they were boond to accept the assurance proposals, let them submit like men, but go on fighting till they got the Act amended .0 that they , could not sign it front 111101. A resolution that they stand by the Act was carried unanimously.
